green-beans-fresh-cooked-fat-added-ns-as.title: Green beans, fresh, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans (string beans) are the edible pods of the common bean plant, usually consumed after cooking. In this form they are fresh, boiled and prepared with added fat, which raises their energy value and gives a richer flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are young pods harvested before the seeds inside fully develop.
Brief cooking (steaming, blanching) retains most of the vitamin C, while prolonged heating can cause some loss.
Adding a small amount of fat (vegetable oil or butter) improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and K.
In many countries green beans are also called snap peas or string beans.
A classic French preparation is green beans sautéed in butter with shallots.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Source of vitamins C and K
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, while vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate (vitamin B9) is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in green beans help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Improved fat‑soluble vitamin absorption
items.content: The added fat makes vitamins A and K more bioavailable.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to legumes.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High intake may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: If the beans are seasoned with salt, total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked beans can contain phytohemagglutinin, a toxin, so they must be fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Green beans can be served as a side dish, tossed into salads, stews, pasta, or baked casseroles. When cooking with fat, use 1–2 tablespoons of oil or butter per 200 g of beans.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pods in the refrigerator in a perforated bag for 3‑5 days. Cooked beans stored in an airtight container last up to 4 days in the fridge or can be frozen for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn, chocolate coated, is an airy corn snack covered with a thin layer of sweet milk or dark chocolate. It combines the crunchy texture of popcorn with a rich chocolate flavor, making it a popular treat for both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate‑coated popcorn first appeared in the United States in the 1970s as a cinema snack.
The chocolate coating can include nuts, caramel, or sea salt for flavor variations.
Plain popcorn is naturally low‑calorie, but the chocolate layer significantly raises its energy content.
Chocolate popcorn is often used in holiday gift packs and as a decorative element in desserts.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Corn kernels are rich in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate, especially dark, is high in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from popcorn and sugar in chocolate provides a rapid energy lift.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Chocolate popcorn can contain a substantial amount of sugar, which is unsuitable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Milk chocolate allergy
items.content: The product may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the chocolate coating, the calorie count is much higher than plain popcorn.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some chocolate coatings may contain trans fats, which should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate‑coated popcorn can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to ice cream, yogurt, or used as a topping for desserts. A brief warm‑up in the microwave makes the chocolate softer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer storage, refrigerate to prevent the chocolate from melting and losing its crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese‑flavored microwave popcorn is a ready‑to‑eat snack that expands in the microwave in 2‑3 minutes. The corn kernels pop into a light, airy texture, while a savory cheese powder coats each piece with a rich, buttery taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks, enjoyed by ancient American civilizations.
Cheese flavor is usually created with a blend of dried dairy solids, flavorings, and spices.
Microwave popcorn hit the market in the 1980s and quickly became popular for its convenience.
A typical bag contains 30‑40 g of ready‑to‑eat popcorn.
Plain popcorn is low‑calorie, but cheese‑flavored versions contain more fat and salt.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet snacks, popcorn contains virtually no sugar, making it a better choice for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Corn kernels are rich in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and polyphenols in popcorn may provide antioxidant effects.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The carbohydrates in popcorn are rapidly digestible, offering a fast energy boost.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Popcorn provides modest amounts of thiamine, niacin, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Cheese‑flavored popcorn often contains a notable amount of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: The cheese powder adds saturated fats that should be limited in a balanced diet.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy may react to the cheese flavoring.

items.title: Risk of overheating
items.content: Overcooking can cause the popcorn to burn and produce potentially harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Microwave the bag according to the package directions (usually 2‑3 minutes), then open and stir to distribute the cheese powder evenly. Enjoy as‑is or sprinkle fresh herbs, spices, or a dash of hot sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened bag in a cool, dry place away from moisture. After opening, transfer any remaining popcorn to an airtight container to maintain crunch and prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Snow cone, no sugar added is a refreshing dessert made from finely shaved ice flavored with natural fruit extracts. No added sugar is used, making it suitable for those monitoring sugar intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first snow cones appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Traditionally they were served in paper cups; today eco‑friendly plastic or glass containers are common.
Sugar‑free versions are often sweetened with stevia or erythritol, but this recipe relies solely on the natural sweetness of fruit.
Ice can be infused with aromatic oils to enhance flavor perception.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Absence of added sugar makes the dessert low‑calorie, suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The large amount of ice helps maintain fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Vitamin boost
items.content: Fruit extracts provide vitamins C and A as well as antioxidants.

items.title: No glycemic spike
items.content: Without sugar, the product avoids rapid blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Cold sensitivity
items.content: Cold desserts can trigger tooth sensitivity or headaches in some individuals.

items.title: Allergy to flavorings
items.content: Fruit extracts may contain trace allergens; people with known sensitivities should check the ingredient list.

items.title: Risk of over‑cooling
items.content: Excessive consumption of very cold foods may lead to feeling overly chilled.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the snow cone immediately after preparation to keep the ice finely shaved. Garnish with fresh berries, mint leaves, or a lime wedge for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared snow cone should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2–3 hours. Ideally, shave the ice right before serving to preserve texture.
